The question now is whether $141 million can cover both the remaining LM26 physics tests and the new commercial engineering program starting in 2027. If one-time listing fees fade and quarterly cash use stays near $11 million, the cash lasts through 2028; if parallel engineering pushes spending higher, the company will need more money sooner. General Fusion, a Canadian developer of clean power from nuclear fusion, went public in July 2026 by merging with Spring Valley Acquisition Corp. III, a blank-check company. Alongside a private share sale, the deal brought in $123.3 million after fees. That cash matters because the business has no revenue and faced tight spending limits last year.

• Cash and short-term investments: $140.9 million on September 30, 2026, up from $49.1 million at the end of 2025
• Total debt: zero after past notes and investment contracts converted into shares
• Third-quarter interest and other income: $1.2 million, up from $0.1 million a year ago

Chief executive Greg Twinney said the cash will "fund our LM26 program through the end of 2028, including our final two milestones, 10 keV, and the Lawson criterion." LM26 is the company's main test machine, and the Lawson criterion is the point where a fusion plasma makes more heat than it loses. In the filing, the fusion developer commits more narrowly that cash covers "at least 12 months from the date of this MD&A."

What to watch: quarterly cash outflow in the full-year 2026 report. If cash use stays near $11 million a quarter, the $140.9 million reserve will last through the 2028 physics tests without another share sale.

🟢 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐇𝐢𝐭 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐇𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭
General Fusion uses Magnetized Target Fusion (MTF), a method that squeezes heated gas with magnetic coils and a metal liner to fuse atoms. Twinney called LM26 the "first fusion machine in the world to achieve 1 keV using practical, low-speed compression." One kiloelectronvolt (1 keV) equals about 10 million degrees Celsius, the first of three physics goals for the machine.

In October, tests verified with the United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority reached 1.1 keV, or 12.6 million degrees Celsius, and internal sensors read 1.2 keV at peak squeeze. Because the method "requires less power, reduces system complexity, and lowers costs," according to Twinney, the group is now upgrading LM26 for its 100-million-degree goal.

What to watch: peer review of the two technical papers submitted on the 1 keV tests and timing for the 10 keV runs. Reaching 10 keV would show the plasma stays stable at ten times the heat.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐬 𝐏𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐇𝐢𝐭
"Our cash use and expenditures since listing have been in line with our expectations, reflecting our disciplined approach to capital efficiency," Twinney said. Yet operating loss excluding one-offs—which removes non-cash stock pay, depreciation, and government grants—more than doubled from a year ago to $11.0 million in the third quarter. By our math, that rose from an average of $9.2 million a quarter in the first half of 2026.

• Research and development excluding stock pay: $5.7 million, up 75% from a year ago by our math
• Research materials and supplies: $1.5 million, up 226% for LM26 machine upgrades
• General and administrative excluding stock pay: $4.3 million, up 173% by our math, as legal and advisory fees rose 889% to $1.9 million

Reported net income of $30.2 million was an accounting quirk caused by $54.9 million of non-cash gains when a lower share price reduced the value of warrant and earnout liabilities. By our math, removing those paper gains and $11.5 million in deal fees leaves a $13.3 million third-quarter loss, and spending will rise further in 2027 when the commercial engineering program starts.

What to watch: general and administrative spending in the fourth quarter of 2026. If overhead does not drop after one-time listing fees fade, higher ongoing costs will shorten the cash runway before 2028.

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐱 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐓𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐬 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭
To close its public listing and private financing, General Fusion issued several layers of preferred stock, warrants, and bonus shares tied to share-price targets. While the company ended September with 53.1 million regular Subordinate Voting Shares, by our math another 69.6 million potential shares sit in convertible securities, warrants, and employee options—equal to 131% of the current regular share count.

• Multiple Voting Shares: 10.4 million shares earning a 12% yearly dividend paid in extra value, redeemable in cash after July 2031
• Warrants: 38.4 million regular warrants plus 2.5 million earnout warrants
• Earnout shares and options: 11.0 million units that convert if the stock reaches $15, $20, and $25
• Employee stock options: 7.3 million options at an average exercise price of $3.75

The Multiple Voting Shares and 10.6 million private-financing warrants carry a six-month price reset in January 2027. If the 20-day average stock price sits below $12.00—it was $7.41 on September 30—the conversion and exercise prices drop as low as $5.00, increasing the shares issued to those holders.

What to watch: the conversion price reset on the twenty-first trading day after January 10, 2027. A reset near the $5.00 floor would More than double the shares owed to preferred holders and private warrant holders.

🔴 𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐥𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐇𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐖𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬
Going public required General Fusion to value complex warrants, earnout shares, and government funding rules under US accounting standards. In its report, the company disclosed that three material weaknesses in its financial reporting controls from 2024 and 2025 remain unresolved as of September 30, 2026.

The group cited a "lack of formalized policies, procedures and controls", weak information-technology controls, and a "lack of qualified personnel" to handle complex debt and government grant accounting. To help fix this, the board appointed David Janashvili as finance chief starting November 30, 2026, and hired outside accounting advisors.

What to watch: the internal control assessment in the 2026 annual report on Form 20-F. Unresolved weaknesses could delay future filings or cause restatements like the one its blank-check partner recorded in early 2026.

General Fusion operates in Canadian dollars in British Columbia but holds most of its new financing cash in US dollars. That mismatch created a $2.1 million currency loss in the third quarter, and a 10% move in the US dollar changes net loss by $3.3 million. Management also warned that rising inflation could lift prices for specialized metals, lab supplies, and engineering staff before commercial revenue begins.

Cash used in operations more than doubled from $14.3 million in the first nine months of 2025. Higher staff counts after last year's layoffs, machine parts for LM26, and public listing bills drove the increase, while cash from government grants dropped as the existing Canadian support deal reached its cap.

𝐆𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟔𝟕.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
This liability tracks warrants owed to the Canadian government's Strategic Response Fund for $55.1 million of cumulative research funding, up from $28.4 million at year-end 2025. Because the fusion group meets its grant rules, it assigns a 99% chance that it will settle this balance with 9.1 million zero-cost warrants rather than cash.

Basic share count rose from 1.5 million a year ago after preferred stock and investment contracts converted into regular shares during the July 2026 listing. Accounting rules also added $70.9 million of non-cash preferred stock adjustments to the loss attributable to common shareholders, resulting in a basic loss of $0.84 per share.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐦 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭?
General Fusion plans to start engineering heat exchangers, liquid metal loops, and power systems in 2027 while still running LM26. Management has not disclosed the annual budget or capital equipment bill for this parallel program.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟏𝟎 𝐤𝐞𝐕 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭?
The roadmap calls for hitting both 10 keV (100 million degrees Celsius) and the Lawson criterion by the end of 2028, and machine upgrades are underway now. Management did not give a target quarter for the 10 keV test runs.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐚𝐬 𝐚 𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲?

One Operator. Five AI Girls. How to Build Virtual Characters Into a Real Business.
Five AI-generated girls. One person behind a laptop. No photographers, no physical studio, and no traditional production crew.
A few years ago, producing content for five different models would have required coordinating locations, equipment, editing teams, and expensive photoshoots.
Today, a single creator can handle much of that process with AI.
But there's a significant difference between generating attractive characters and building a business around them.
You can create 100 beautiful AI images in a day and still earn nothing.
The opportunity isn't in producing more faces. It's in building recognizable personalities, creating content people return for, and developing something an audience or customer is willing to pay for.
If I were starting an AI character studio from zero, I'd approach it as a business with six connected systems.
Here's exactly how I'd structure it.
 
1. Build the Characters: Five Different Identities, Five Different Audience
The first mistake people make is generating five beautiful girls who all look and act almost identical.
Different faces don't automatically create different brands.
Every character needs her own identity, visual direction, personality, and audience.
I'd start with five distinct concepts.
Luna — Fitness & Lifestyle
Gym sessions, workout outfits, wellness routines, and everyday fitness content.
Her audience follows for fitness inspiration, athletic fashion, and recurring lifestyle content.
Mia — Fashion & Luxury
Designer-inspired outfits, city photography, beauty routines, and polished lifestyle visuals.
Her content would focus on fashion discovery, styling, and aspirational aesthetics.
Eva — Gaming & Technology
Gaming setups, headphones, streaming culture, desk transformations, and technology-focused content.
She would appeal to gaming communities and people interested in entertainment and internet culture.
Sofia — Everyday Lifestyle
Coffee shops, casual fashion, travel moments, and personal-style storytelling.
The goal would be familiarity. Content that feels recognizable rather than constantly extravagant.
Aria — Cinematic & Alternative Fashion
Dark outfits, nighttime city scenes, alternative styling, and visually distinctive photography.
Her advantage would be a recognizable aesthetic that separates her from mainstream lifestyle creators.
The goal isn't to make every character appeal to everyone.
It's to give each one a specific reason to exist.
Building visual consistency
Before publishing, I'd create a reference library for every character.
That means consistent facial features, hairstyles, wardrobe guidelines, recurring locations, and visual examples.
A character shouldn't look completely different every time someone opens her profile.
I'd also define how each fictional personality communicates and clearly disclose its AI-generated nature.
Your first move: Create five character profiles and produce ten consistent images for each before worrying about growth.
 
2. Build the Content System: Make Production Repeatable
Creating one impressive image is easy compared with producing reliable content every week.
A business needs a workflow.
Without one, every new post becomes another experiment.
You waste time rewriting prompts, fixing inconsistent faces, choosing random locations, and generating content that never gets published.
I'd organize the entire production process into five stages.
Stage 1 — Planning
Build a weekly content calendar for each character.
Decide which posts are designed for discovery, which develop the character, and which introduce a product or offer.
Stage 2 — Image production
Use tools such as FLUX, Midjourney, or ComfyUI to produce character-consistent visuals.
Generate variations, compare the results, and save the strongest outputs.
Stage 3 — Video production
Use video-generation tools to turn selected visual concepts into short clips.
Simple scenes often work better than overly complicated sequences.
Walking through a city, sitting at a desk, preparing coffee, or changing outfits can provide useful recurring formats.
Stage 4 — Editing
Prepare each image and video for its intended platform.
A vertical video for TikTok and an image post for X shouldn't automatically use the same packaging.
Stage 5 — Publishing and review
Schedule posts, review performance, and record which concepts deserve additional production.
The production economics
Suppose a solo operator spends 20 hours per week creating and managing content for five characters.
That's approximately 80 hours over four weeks.
At a hypothetical operating budget of $250 per month, software spending alone would average around $3.13 per working hour.
That figure excludes the operator's labor, hardware, taxes, payment processing, and other business expenses.
The important point is understanding the cost of producing usable assets, not just how many images a subscription allows you to generate.
Your first move: Build one production workflow that can consistently deliver photos and short videos for every character without starting from scratch.
 
3. Grow the Audience: Attractive Images Are Only the Beginning
One of the biggest misconceptions about AI influencers is that realistic visuals automatically produce followers.
They don't.
An image may generate attention without giving anyone a reason to follow the account.
Growth requires recognizable content formats and a clear audience.
I'd test three types of posts for every character.
Discovery content
Short videos and images built around visually interesting moments.
A fitness character might feature an unusual workout scene.
A fashion character might show a distinctive outfit in a recognizable city environment.
A gaming character might appear in a visually impressive setup.
The objective is attracting new viewers.
Personality content
Posts that make the character recognizable.
Recurring routines, fictional stories, visual preferences, and themed series help people understand what kind of content to expect.
The identity needs continuity.
Community content
Posts that invite genuine participation.
Outfit comparisons, gaming preferences, visual concept choices, and questions about upcoming content can reveal what the audience actually enjoys.
The objective is repeat engagement rather than collecting empty impressions.
What I'd measure
I wouldn't evaluate an account by views alone.
I'd track profile visits, follower conversion, returning viewers, shares, saves, and engagement quality.
Consider two hypothetical videos.
Video A receives 500,000 views and generates 250 followers.
Video B receives 100,000 views and generates 600 followers.
Video A has more reach.
Video B converts viewers into followers at twelve times the rate.
That distinction matters if the objective is building an audience rather than collecting occasional viral posts.
Your first move: Test three recurring formats per character, measure their results, and increase production of the formats that consistently attract returning followers.

 
4. Monetize the Attention: Build Offers Before Chasing Millions of Followers
A large following is not automatically a profitable business.
An account with 500,000 followers can struggle to generate revenue.
A much smaller audience can support a profitable offer if its members genuinely want the product or service.
I'd build monetization around four areas.
A. Paid memberships
Offer subscribers additional original content, early access to creative releases, behind-the-scenes production material, and community benefits.
The offer should be transparent about the characters being fictional and AI-generated.
For example, consider a hypothetical $9 monthly membership.

These figures are revenue illustrations, not actual earnings or forecasts. They exclude fees, refunds, taxes, churn, and operating expenses.
Getting those subscribers is the hard part.
B. Brand collaborations
Virtual characters can feature original promotional concepts, digital fashion campaigns, product demonstrations, and branded visual content.
A gaming character could be useful for promoting accessories.
A fitness character could support sportswear campaigns.
A fashion character could participate in digital clothing showcases.
The value comes from audience fit, creative quality, and clear commercial disclosure.
C. AI content production services
This may be one of the most practical routes for an operator who hasn't built a large audience yet.
Instead of selling access to a character, sell the production capability itself.
A small business could purchase:
Product visuals
Short promotional videos
Virtual spokesperson concepts
Creative variations for advertising
Consistent AI character development
A hypothetical $500 content package sold to four clients would generate $2,000 in gross revenue.
That's a more concrete sales target than assuming social media views will turn into money on their own.
D. Digital products
Once the workflow is tested, useful parts of it can be packaged into products.
Character design guides, prompt libraries, production templates, content calendars, and technical tutorials.
The important part is selling something that genuinely helps the customer.
Your first move: Choose one primary revenue model and create a small, clearly priced offer before investing heavily in scaling.
 
5. Analyze What Works: Stop Guessing and Start Measuring
This is where the project starts becoming a real operation.
I'd build one dashboard covering all five characters.
Every week, I'd compare audience performance, production costs, and commercial results.
Not every character deserves the same investment.
A character generating 1 million views could be less commercially valuable than another generating 100,000 views.
What matters is the relationship between attention, operating costs, and revenue.
The five metrics I'd prioritize
1. Cost per finished asset
How much does it cost to generate and edit one usable photo or video?
Include failed generations and editing time.
2. Follower conversion rate
How effectively does content turn profile visitors or viewers into followers?
3. Returning audience
Are people coming back to see the character again?
4. Revenue per paying customer
How much revenue does each customer generate over a defined period?
5. Contribution margin
After variable production and transaction costs, how much revenue remains to cover fixed expenses and profit?

The $2,150 remaining after listed direct costs isn't necessarily net profit. It would still need to cover additional business expenses, taxes, and the operator's labor.
But now there is a basis for decision-making.
Instead of generating more content for the biggest account, the operator can investigate which audience and offer produce the strongest business results.

6. Build the Real Business: From Five Profiles to One Digital Studio
The biggest opportunity isn't necessarily owning five AI influencer accounts.
It's owning a reliable system that can create, manage, and monetize digital characters.
Think about what the operator actually develops throughout the process.

The character accounts become part of the portfolio demonstrating the studio's capabilities.
The product side
Reusable templates, educational resources, and production systems developed from actual experience.
These could serve customers who prefer to build their own projects instead of hiring the studio.
When I'd scale
I wouldn't automatically launch another five characters.
I'd first establish whether the existing operation can consistently generate enough revenue to cover its costs and compensate the operator.
Then I'd document repeatable processes, improve quality control, and outsource specific tasks where doing so makes financial sense.
The objective is not managing the largest possible number of virtual personalities.
It's building an operation where additional output doesn't require a proportional increase in time and expense.
That is what makes a production system scalable.
Your first move: Prove that one character or one studio offer can consistently generate real customer demand before adding unnecessary complexity.
The Final Perspective
One person working from a laptop can now produce types of visual content that once required a traditional creative team.
That's a meaningful change.
But access to powerful tools doesn't remove the need for judgment, marketing, production discipline, or customer demand.
AI can generate the characters.
It can accelerate production.
It can help create content at a scale that would previously have been difficult for an individual.
What it cannot guarantee is an interested audience or a profitable business.
Those still need to be earned.
The most valuable part of an AI character studio isn't the number of beautiful faces on its monitors.
It's the system behind them: recognizable identities, repeatable production, audience relationships, commercially useful offers, and measurable results.
The characters attract attention. The system determines whether that attention becomes a business.

article.plain_text:
GTA 6 drops this Thursday. Most of the money around it this week will go to people who never finish the story.
Film your own street on a phone. Twenty seconds later @Picsart hands it back looking like a frame from the game -- neon dusk, wet asphalt, palm trees, that Vice City haze. No console, no copy of the game and no editing skills...
 
Clips like this already pull millions of views, and the game is not even out yet. Rockstar told The Hollywood Reporter that trailer 2 hit 475M views in 24 hours. In the last 7 days the top 30 GTA 6 posts on X collected 66.5M views, and a single post took 29.4M of them.
That attention pays twice. TikTok and YouTube pay for the views, and Picsart pays on top through its Earn program. 
Below is the full setup: five ways to get paid, every prompt I use, and one folder where Fable 5.2 runs all of it through Picsart while you do something else.
Open Picsart in the next tab and build along with me -> Click here 
The whole article fits in one line.
You film or play. Fable 5.2 directs. @Picsart restyles, cuts, finishes and pays.
 
00 / The 10-minute setup
 
The stack has two parts. 
Fable 5.2 is the director: it looks at your footage, picks the moments, writes every prompt, title, caption and hashtag. 
Picsart is the hands: 150+ video, image and audio models behind one connection, plus the clipper, the captions and the payouts.
They talk through MCP, so Fable calls Picsart tools by itself and you never copy files between tabs. In Claude Code it is one command.
 
In claude.ai it is even shorter: open Connectors, find Picsart Media Studio and press "+".
 
The first test costs nothing. Ask Fable which Picsart models accept your own video as input and what a clip will cost.
 
Fable comes back with a short list, a recommendation and a credit quote. Picsart quotes the price before anything runs, so you always see the cost of a batch before you say "Go".
 
01 / Method 1: Real life -> GTA 6
 
This is the method with the lowest entry and the loudest result. You need a phone and three shots from your day: you walking to your car, a gas station at night, a friend passing on a scooter.
Picsart keeps the motion and repaints the world. The people move exactly as they moved, the car takes the same turn, and everything around them becomes a high-end open-world game at sunset.
 
The look is a recipe with four parts: light, palette, surface, camera. I keep it in one file so every clip from every day looks like the same game.
 
Then Fable gets one prompt for the whole folder. It reads each shot, trims it, restyles it through Picsart and hands back a batch.
 
Some footage restyles better than the rest, and after a few batches the pattern is obvious.
 Cars, gas stations, parking lots and street corners work best.
 Evening light beats noon every time.
 One clear subject in motion beats a crowded frame.
 A slow pan or a locked phone beats a shaky run.
One detail decides the money here. A restyled shot runs up to 20 seconds, and TikTok pays only for videos longer than 60 seconds. Four shots in a row make one 61-second video that qualifies, and the same four shots go out separately to Shorts, Reels and X.
Post these as "I turned my street into GTA 6". That line gets shared because people want to try it on their own street.
 
02 / Method 2: Real life vs GTA 6
 
This format already took 2.6M views on a single post. Real footage on one side, the game on the other, and the viewer does the rest of the work.
 
You already own both halves after Method 1. After Thursday the format gets a second life: a real Miami corner next to its Vice City twin from your own gameplay.
Ideas that write themselves:
 My commute vs GTA 6.
 My gym vs GTA 6.
 Ocean Drive, real vs game.
 My city at 2 am vs Vice City at 2 am. 
 
Comparison clips win on two numbers. People rewatch them to compare, and they argue in the comments about which side looks better. Rewatches and comments are what every algorithm rewards, and Picsart Earn counts them too.
 
03 / Method 3: The in-game phone
 
Look at how Rockstar cut the trailers. Half of the memorable moments are vertical clips filmed by people inside the world, on their phones. The audience already reads GTA 6 through a phone screen.
 
So after release you package gameplay the same way. A moment from your recording becomes a post made by someone who lives in that city: cropped vertical, a caption in character, a made-up username, a comment that starts a fight.
Examples of how it reads:
 "My Uber driver just did this on the bridge".
 "Gator in the pool again. Third time this week".
 "Rate my neighbor's parking".
 
These clips are short, cheap to make and endless. One evening of free roam gives you material for a week.
 
04 / Method 4: Clip your own gameplay
 
You play for two hours and press record. That is your whole job in this method. The recording goes into the folder, and Fable finds the money inside it.
Picsart sends Fable frames from the recording with timestamps, so it reads the whole session in a couple of minutes. It scores every moment and writes them into a table.
 
 
Take one line from that table: "01:12:40 - 01:13:25, chaos, golf cart survives a five-star chase, score 9". That line becomes four videos, one for each platform.
The cut itself is the easy part, and thousands of people will post the same raw moment. What separates a clip that pays from a clip that gets flagged as reused content is five layers on top of the footage.
 Hook -- a line on screen in the first second, written about this exact moment.
 Take -- your opinion in one sentence.
 Captions -- your own style, word by word.
 Recut -- the payoff teased first, then the build-up.
 Close -- a question that splits the comments.
Raw clip: 40 seconds of a police chase. With the layers: "I tried to outrun five stars in a golf cart" on screen, a 1.5-second teaser of the crash, the chase, and "Would you have jumped?" at the end. Same footage, a different video.
 
YouTube adds one rule that most clippers will learn the expensive way. If the first 7 seconds show graphic violence, the video gets no ads. Seconds 8 to 15 mean limited ads, and after 15 seconds it monetizes normally.
So every clip starts with the drive, the dialogue or the reaction, and the hit lands later. Fable checks this before anything ships.
 
 
05 / Method 5: The weekly long video
 
Short clips bring the reach. The long video brings the rate. YouTube Shorts pay around $0.03-0.10 per 1,000 views, and long gaming videos pay around $2-3, which is at least 20 times more for the same view.
You do not film anything new for it. Once a week Fable takes your ten best clips, pulls the full moments from the source recordings and builds one 8-12 minute video with chapters.
Titles that fit the format:
 "GTA 6 Week 1: 10 moments the trailers did not show".
 "I turned 10 real places into GTA 6".
 
 
06 / The math
 
Here is the model I run before I commit to anything. Three clips a day, one long video a week, public rates only.
 
 
 20K average views per clip -> $494 - $1,200 a month.
 100K average views per clip -> $2,470 - $6,000 a month.
 500K average views per clip -> $11,950 - $29,400 a month.
These are models from published rates, and your numbers depend on your views. 
The gates are simple: TikTok Creator Rewards wants 10K followers and videos over 60 seconds, YouTube wants 1,000 subscribers. Launch week is the fastest way through both gates you will get this year.

07 / The engine: one folder
 
Five methods sound like five jobs. In practice it is one folder and one prompt a day.
 
STUDIO.md is the file that turns Fable from a chatbot into your editor. It holds your formats, your lengths per platform, your caption style and the list of things that never ship.
 
Every day you drop new material into inbox and send one prompt.
 
 
What comes back is a package per platform: the video, the title, the caption, the hashtags and the first comment, with every check already passed.
 
Your part is to watch the result and tap publish. That tap stays with you on purpose, because an account that posts with a human eye on it lives longer.
 
08 / The second check: Picsart Earn
 
Everything above gets paid by the platforms. The same videos can get paid one more time, because they were made with Picsart.
Picsart Earn has no follower minimum. It pays on views, comments, shares and reach across Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and X, and the program paid out more than $1M in under 100 days. Campaigns go up to $5 per 1,000 views.
Picsart's own example makes it concrete: at $2 per 1,000 views, a clip with 50K views is $100. That is on top of whatever TikTok or YouTube paid for the same clip.
For a new account this matters more than anything else in the article. The platforms make you wait for 1,000 subscribers or 10K followers. Earn pays while you are still at zero.

09 / Launch week
 
The window is short and it opens on Thursday. Here is how I would spend it.
Before Thursday -- film 10 real shots, restyle them, post Method 1 and Method 2 daily.
Thursday -- play and record 2-3 hours, ship the first three gameplay clips the same night.
Friday to Sunday -- three clips a day, mix all four short methods.
Monday -- the first weekly long video.
Wednesday -- read the numbers, keep the two formats that worked, drop the rest.
 
The first days after a release this size reward speed. The accounts that post on day one get the search traffic that everyone else fights over for months.
 
Conclusion
 
GTA 6 is the biggest entertainment launch of the decade, and the attention around it is already measured in hundreds of millions of views. A share of that attention goes to whoever shows up with clips this week.
You do not need a studio for it. You need a phone or a controller, one folder, Fable 5.2 to direct and @Picsart to restyle, cut, finish and pay.
